rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figs. 4-7 report the authors' own set-up of an automated sensor-based irrigation control system (15 TDT probes, piezometers, datalogger, management software) in the Padova Botanical Garden and monitoring data from the first irrigation season (June-September 2000).
rows.notes: The study is a primary case study of soil-moisture-sensor automated irrigation control (management software plus datalogger) under sprinkler irrigation. Its own results concern technical performance: the system terminated irrigation when rainfall raised moisture above the 32% full point, reset go-ahead 6 days after rain, sensors responded within 2 min, and the 'average' criterion maintained matric potential above -75 kPa in MS4 but penalised plants with higher needs. Irrigation volumes applied (>450 mm, 200-250 mm) are reported but no comparison with a non-automated baseline and no quantified water savings or irrigation optimisation are given; the authors do not frame results as water conservation. Hence the study demonstrates that the automation functioned (a precondition of water conservation) rather than the claimed water-conservation effect; marked upstream. Whether 2002-era workstation control software counts as 'app_scheduling' is also loose, but treated as the same technology class (software-based automated scheduling). No independent second method on water saving, no multi-site evaluation (one garden), scale is a 2 ha garden split into six macro-sectors, limitations stated concern the 'average' criterion and sensor number rather than a water-conservation result, and the only dispersion reported (Table 1 S.D.) concerns retention curves not the claimed effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figs. 4-7 report the authors' own automated irrigation control system and first-year monitoring data from the Padova Botanical Garden.
rows.notes: The irrigation network studied consists of about 550 sprinklers controlled by 27 solenoid valves (Section 2.2); drip irrigation is not used or tested anywhere in the study. The study therefore provides no evidence of its own on drip irrigation, let alone drip-related water conservation. Technology mismatch. Additionally, even for the sprinkler automation actually studied, no water savings are quantified (see other row).

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a single-site technical case study of sensor-based automated irrigation scheduling under sprinkler irrigation in a 2 ha botanical garden; it reports system performance and soil-water status, not water-use savings relative to any baseline.
